2. Succinctly, the facts of the case, as stated in the writ petition, are that the Bera Pourashava is situated in the Upazilla of Bera under the District of Pabna and the election of the said Pourashava was lastly held in March, 1999 when Mr Md Abdul Baten was elected its Chairman together with the prescribed number of Commissioners. They had assumed the responsibility of administering the Bera Pourashava for a period of five years, as per the Provisions of Often স্থানীয় সরকার (পৌরসভা) আইন, ২০০৯ (hereinafter referred to as the “পৌরসভা আইন” But even after expiry of their 5-year tenure, they have been continuing to run the administration of the said Pourashava by holding their portfolios without arranging for any election. The respondents, particularly, the Election Commission and the Ministry of Local Government and Rural Development (respondent Nos. 1 and 2 respectively) were under a legal obligation to hold the election of the Bera Pourashava after the expiry of five years in the year 2004, but till date no election has been held. Under the circumstances, the petitioner, as the voter of the Bera Pourashava and a conscious citizen of the land, approached this Court for vindication of his legal right and obtained this Rule. 

 8. We have perused the materials on record and considered the above submissions and the relevant Constitutional as well as statutory provisions and the case laws as mentioned above. 

 9. In the case at hand, it transpires that the election of the Bera Pourashava was last held in March, 1999 and, accordingly, the five years tenure elapsed in March, 2004. However, from the averments of the writ petition it appears that before the expiry of the said five years two writ petitions were filed before this Court challenging the curtailment of the area and boundary of the Bera Pourashava and both the writ petitions have been finally disposed of by the Apex Court on 7-6-2011 keeping the area intact and nullifying the curtailment. Therefore, at the moment, there is no legal impediment to arrange for the election of the Bera Pourashava with its area and boundary as it stood before issuance of the notice of the said curtailment. 

 10. With the above factual background of the instant case, the pertinent questions that come up for consideration is whether there is any legal obligation on the part of the respondents to hold the election of the Bera Pourashava and, if so, who is it to arrange the said election; is it the Government or the Election Commission or both of them jointly. The other questions are whether the petitioner possesses sufficient standing to seek a writ of mandamus and whether this Court should issue a writ of mandamus upon the respondents directing them to hold election of the Bera Pourashava. 

 34. Even in cases where the power is conferred in enabling terms, judicial decisions have affirmed this principle in clearer terms. The locus classics on the subject is the decision of the House of Lords in Julius vs Lord Bishop of Oxford, (1880) 5 AC 214 which has received approval of the Supreme Court of India in L. Hirday Narain vs Income Tax Officer, Bareilly, (AIR 1971 SC 33). 

 35. The statute in that case said that "it shall be lawful" for a Bishop to issue a commission of enquiry in case of an alleged misconduct by a clergyman either on the application of a complainant or of his own motion. In the context of such statutory language it was held that it merely conferred a power. 

 "But there may be something in the nature of the thing empowered to be done, something in the object for which it is to be done, something in the conditions under which it is to be done, something in the title of the person or persons for whose benefit the power is to be exercised, which may couple the power with a duty, and make it the duty of the person on whom the power is reposed to exercise that power when called upon to do so the cases to which I have referred appear to decide nothing more than that where a power is deposited with a public officer for the purpose of being used for the benefit of persons who are specifically pointed out, and with regard to whom a definition is supplied by the legislature of the conditions upon which they are entitled to call for its exercise, that power ought to be exercised, as the Court will require it to be exercised." 

 37. In the same case of the House of Lords in Julius vs Lord Bishop of Oxford, (1880) 5 AC Lord Penzaance said at page 229: 

 38. In the same case of the House of Lords in Julius vs Lord Bishop of Oxford, (1880) 5 AC Lord Blackburn said at the pages 241 and 244: 

 39. In Hirday Narain's case (Supra) the Supreme Court of India observed as follows: 

 “If a statute invests a public officer with authority to do an act in a specified set of circumstances, it is imperative upon him to exercise his authority in a manner appropriate to the case when a party interested and having right to apply moves in that behalf and circumstances for exercise of authority are shown to exist. Even if their words used in the statute are prima-facie enabling, the Courts will readily infer a duty to exercise power which is invested in aid of enforcement of a right-public or private of a citizen." 

 41. From the examination carried out so far it transpires that the present case stands on a better and much higher footing inasmuch as section 21(1) concurrently read with sections 8 and 20(2)(ছ) of the পৌরসভা আইন do not only confer an enabling or discretionary power, but it also imposes a statutory duty upon the Election Commission to hold an election in terms. Having regard to the object and purpose of the statute and the language in which the duty is imposed, there is no manner of doubt that its enforcement can be secured by the issue of an appropriate writ. 

 42. While in India there is abundance of cases to refer to and to rely on for seeking mandamus form the High Courts for compelling the State-functionaries to hold elections of the Pourashavas, in our jurisdiction we could not trace out any such cases in which our Courts have intervened and directed the State if functionaries holding of an election. 

 43. Given this scenario; we feel it pertinent to reproduce some observations of the case of Budha Mal vs State of Punjab (1967) Punj LR 974, facts of which are almost similar to the present case. In this case the Municipal Election Rules, 1952, enacted under the Punjab Municipal Act, 1911, prescribed the mode and procedure for holding municipal election. Rule 63 prescribed grounds for declaring an election void. The Election Commissioner was constituted the competent authority to hold an enquiry into the validity of an election, if challenged. Under Rule 63 read with section 254, if any one or more of the grounds for declaring an election void was established at the enquiry, the Election commissioner was required to submit to the State Government a report that the election of the returned candidate be declared to be void. Rule 69 provided that, under such circumstances, the Election Commissioner or the Punjab Government, as the case may be, shall direct that a new election shall be held. Section 255 required the State Government to pass the necessary orders on receiving the report of the Election Commissioner and such orders were to be notified in the official Gazette. In this case, therefore, the report was made by the Election Commissioner on 6-11-1966 declaring the election of a returned candidate as null and void and the consequential notification issued by the State Government on 23-3-1967 was duly published in the official gazette. No direction was, however, issued by the Election Commissioner or the State Government for holding a new election for several months. 

 44. One of the questions raised for decision in that case related to the mandatory duty cast upon the Election Commissioner or the Punjab Government, as the case may be, to hold a new election under such circumstances and the relief sought was to compel the performance of such duty. 

 In such a contingency, as has occurred in the instant case, the democratic functioning remains suspended, and all this, because of the remissness of the executive. 

 The Municipal Committee as well as those for whose benefit the institution of the local Government is intended is entitled to the judgment, intelligence, experience, guidance and counsel for the elected representatives of the people in the constituency. The executive in this case has deprived a section of the community from the services of its elected representatives. The inordinate delay in not inviting the electors to choose their nominees cannot but be deprecated, especially when it has remained unexplained and was avoidable. 

 The statutory right to elect candidates for municipal constituency could not, either directly or indirectly, be denied or abridged, but the non-compliance with the statutory provisions has, in this case, violated the exercise of their right, and, till the constituency is called to elect its representative, the franchise stands abridged. The voter in this constituency has been shut off from the ballot box, which is obnoxious to the statutory guarantee of the right to vote. 

 In this case, there is a statutory obligation to hold election. Even if law were to afford no remedy for enforcing it, there is imposed a duty upon this court to remedy the wrong and interfere by mandamus. 

 In a case, like the present, the duty to hold an election was ministerial in its character, and there is no controversy as to the existence of the conditions upon which the call of the election was founded. The officer responsible, or the State Government, can be compelled by mandamus to make the call and hold election. Mandamus, in the circumstances, is an appropriate remedy to compel performance by officers and by the state, of their duty with respect to the holding of an election. 

 The State whose duty for holding election is purely ministerial, can, in an appropriate case, be compelled to act by a writ of mandamus. This court is not without power to issue mandamus in a case, like the present where, in consequence of laches,  the holding of an election has been unduly delayed. 

 48. In a similar situation, the Nagpur High Court in the case of Gopal Jairam vs State of Madhya Pradesh AIR (38)1951 Nagpur 181 issued writ of mandamus upon the State Government to hold election for Nagpur Municipal Committee where after dissolving the committee in the year 1942 the Government was delaying the election of the Municipality year after year and was running its affairs by the administrators, appointing one after another. 

 49. In the case of Hargovind Tamraker vs State AIR 1986 Madhya Pradesh 63 the Hutta Municipal Council's tenure ended in 1979 and since then the body was being run by the administrators and lastly by the impugned unelected (appointed) committed and upon examining the legality of the appointment of the said 'committee the Madhya Pradesh High Court not only quashed the appointment of the committee, but also directed the Government to hold election for the Municipal Council, Hutta under District Damoh. 

 53. In the case at hand, the tenure of the Bera Pourashava ended in the year 2004 but no step was taken by the Election Commission or the Government to hold the election for the said Pourashava. An excuse might have been pleaded by the Election Commission of the Government, had they appeared before this Court and contested the Rule, that due to the pendency of two writ petitions they could not proceed with the holding of the said election but it would not sustain for two reasons. Firstly, as transpires from the statements of the writ petition, there was no order of injunction from this Court debarring the Election Commission or the Government to refrain from holding the said election and, secondly, for the sake of argument even if it is accepted that they did not proceed towards holding the election of the Bera Pourashava because of the Court being in session of the matter, however, after the said cases being finally disposed of by the Apex Court on 7-6-2011, there was no reason for the Election Commission and the Government to hold the election of the Bera Pourashava. Given the above scenario of the case, this Court is inclined to direct respondent Nos.1 and 2 to take necessary steps for holding election of the Bera Pourashava immediately. 

 54. Before parting with this judgment, this Court regrettably records that the vital respondents of this case, namely the Ministry of LGRD and the Election Commission, did not bother to appear before this Court. This Court by their presence could have been effectively assisted and, thereby, greatly benefitted in fully and successfully disposing of the present case as they are somewhat acquainted and relatively conversant with the different provisions of law relating to election matters in addition to possessing the practical knowledge and experiences in dealing with election of local Governments. They could have provided this Court with the real information as to the reason for delay in holding the election of the different local Government bodies across the country and, in particular, how the Government and the Election Commission work in initiating the elections of the local Governments. 

 55. While this Court has sought to strengthen the position and power of the Election Commission vide the numerous judgments, in future, in an appropriate case it would not hesitate to castigate the failures of the said Commission in timely conducting the elections of any local body which occurred in the fate of the Bera Pourashava. Also, the tendency of the Election Commission as to not handling its cases pending before this Court might be an appropriate matter to be deprecated by this Court, if the repetition of the same is noticed by this Court in another case. It is expected that the Election Commission being an independent Constitutional body ought to have more vigilance in dealing with its litigations pending before the Supreme Court. In the case of Jamaluddin vs Major General Abdus Salam, 66 DLR 362 (relevant para 34) this Court suggested some guidance and the courses for the Election Commission to assist this Court in dealing with the cases where they have been made party. It is deplorable that this Court, as of today, is not aware of any step taken by the Election Commission towards resolution of the difficulties it has been encountering in adjudication upon the cases filed by the litigants against the Election Commission.
